Pixel
Each pixel is described by three numbers: (Red, Green, Blue)

the first number tells us how much red light the pixel emits,
the second how much green light it emits,
and the third how much blue light it emits.

Each RGB value is a number from 0 to 255.
0 = none of that color
255 = maximum amount of that color

units.label: slide 16
units.text:
Mpx
More Mpx can mean more detail, but it does not automatically mean a better photo.

Mpx describes the image resolution, not necessarily the amount of real detail captured.
12 Mpx means the camera can produce an image with about 12 million pixels.

units.label: slide 17
units.text:
The image is the pixels.
The file format decides how to store them.

Examples:
BMP
PNG
JPEG / JPG
SVG

Same image, different file size.
Image vs Image File

units.label: slide 18
units.text:
BMP files usually store raw pixel data without major compression, which keeps image quality high but results in large file sizes.
.BMP

units.label: slide 19
units.text:
.PNG= Portable Network Graphics
stores the image as pixels (Raster)
uses lossless compression
after opening the file, the original pixel values can be reconstructed exactly
very good at compressing areas with repeated or similar colors
Best for:
screenshots
logos
diagrams
Graphics with Transparency

Not ideal for photographs because the file can become quite large.
PNG saves space without throwing away image information.

units.label: slide 20
units.text:
.JPEG (JPG)
stores the image as pixels (Raster)
uses lossy compression
removes some image information to reduce file size
works especially well for photographs and smooth color gradients
Best for: photographs and web images

units.label: slide 21
units.text:
.JPEG (JPG)
https://www.disk-project.eu/web/sv/do-you-know-jpg-compression/
Psychovisual compression
	JPEG takes advantage of how our eyes work:
	We notice changes in brightness and detail more than small changes in color.

	So JPEG can store color information less precisely while keeping the image 	looking almost the same to us.

	This is called psychovisual compression — removing information that humans 	are less likely to notice.

JPEG makes files smaller by sacrificing some image accuracy, especially information our eyes are less sensitive to.

units.label: slide 22
units.text:
. SVG  = Scalable Vector Graphics 
SVG is fundamentally different from PNG and JPEG (Raster X Vector image).
Instead of storing every pixel, it stores instructions for drawing shapes like:
lines
circles
rectangles
curves
text
Because the shapes are calculated again whenever the image is displayed, SVG can be enlarged without becoming pixelated.
Best for:
logos
icons
diagrams
Not suitable for normal photographs.

units.label: slide 23
units.text:
How Can We Make Images Smaller?
Reduce the resolutionFewer pixels = less data to store.
Reduce the number of colorsUse fewer possible color values or a smaller color palette.
Use lossless compressionStore repeated patterns more efficiently without losing information.Example: PNG
Use lossy compressionRemove some less noticeable image information.Example: JPEG
Choose the right file formatDifferent formats are better for different types of images.

units.label: slide 24
units.text:
Green Screen / Blue Screen
How does it work?
The computer checks the RGB values of each pixel.
If a pixel is close to the chosen screen color, it is removed or made transparent.
A new background is then placed behind the subject.
Example:
(20, 230, 30) → very green → probably part of the green screen.

Why Green and Blue, but not Red?

units.label: slide 25
units.text:
Why green?
camera sensors capture green very well
green is usually very different from human skin tones
it gives a clean separation from the person
Why blue?
Blue screen works the same way and is useful when:
the subject is wearing green
the scene contains green objects
Why not red?
Red is much closer to skin tones, lips, and many natural colors, so removing red could accidentally remove parts of the person.
